Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Sotah 9b: ‘GEMARA: The Sages taught (Tosefta 3:15): Samson rebelled with his eyes, as it is stated: “Then his father and his mother said to him: Is there never a woman among the daughters of your brethren, or among all my people, that you go out to take a wife of the uncircumcised Philistines? And Samson said to his father: Get her for me; for she is pleasant in my eyes” (Judges 14:3). Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: Inasmuch as he was rooted in the mystery of Circles: his mother being from Judah and his father from Dan, as I wrote above. And this is: 'for she is pleasing in my eyes' (Judges 14:3), concerning which our Sages expounded (Sotah 9b): Samson followed his eyes, etc.; the meaning being: he was extraordinarily elevated in his spiritual vision, namely there was such sublime holiness within his eyes, that he reasoned: since she is pleasing in my eyes, surely such is the will of Hashem, blessed be He.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: And in mundane affairs man can forget the blessed Creator, boasting “my power and the might of my hand”; therefore they required the dark/blue consuming fire which is close to man, training him not to claim self-made power, for Hashem wills the toil of your hands. And this explains the Zohar (Mishpatim 101a): “Initially Mother, and then Wife” — meaning that Hashem drew away the light and independent strength from her until she required that light be imparted to her.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Genesis 27:1: ‘When Isaac was old and his eyes were too dim to see, he called his older son Esau and said to him, “My son.” He answered, “Here I am.”’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:46, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Genesis 27:1) to illuminate his teaching here (“And it is said: “and his eyes were dim so that he could not see”, and our Sages expounded: on account of the smoke of the incense offered by Esau's wives, because the terror of his penetrating gaze did not strike...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.

And on this account the Zohar states (Bereishit 27b): “Whoever becomes angry is as if he worshiped idols,” because he arrogates unto himself an alien power, imagining himself as a master possessing sovereign domain of his own.

Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 1:25
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: And this is likewise the matter brought in the Talmud (Chagigah 26a): that the Showbread made by the house of Garmu never mouldered, because they heated from within and baked from within; and they brought artisans from Alexandria of Egypt and the bread they made became moldy, because they heated from without and baked from without; to bake they knew just like the house of Garmu, yet they did not know how to remove it from the oven like them, and the bread they made broke.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Genesis 20:16: ‘And to Sarah he said, “I herewith give your brother a thousand pieces of silver; this will serve you as vindication before all who are with you, and you are cleared before everyone.”’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:46, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Genesis 20:16) to illuminate his teaching here (“This was caused by Abimelech saying to her: “Behold, he is to you a covering of the eyes”, implying that she required a covering of the eyes as noted, giving room for scoffers to say: the child is from Abimelech, and...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And perforce, as I wrote, he means that which is called, by Hashem and the Torah and the Israel who walk in His footsteps, “beauty in the body”; and this is through the fear [of God], as it says, “so that His fear be [upon your faces]” (Shemos 20:17), and it says, “for I said, only there is no fear of God [in this place]” (Bereishis 20:11) — for the fear of God nullifies evil desires.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: Such was the Generation of the Flood receiving boundless bounty, saying: “Depart from us... what is Shaddai that we should serve Him”; That is, the Name Shaddai indicates boundaries, as stated in the Talmud (Chagigah 12a): that He said to His world “Enough” (dai), for it was expanding and going like two spools of warp, etc.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Genesis 21:9: ‘Sarah saw the son whom Hagar the Egyptian had borne to Abraham playing.’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:47, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Genesis 21:9) to illuminate his teaching here (“Genesis 21:9 “The son of Hagar the Egyptian, whom she had borne unto Abraham, mocking”, as written in Shemot Rabbah 1:1: that Abraham was the cause in that he spared his rod, therefore Scripture attributed the youth...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And this is the sign of visitation: when this faith enters the heart that the Holy One, blessed be He, visits and watches over. Wherefore visitation is ascribed primarily to Sarah, even though it applied to Abraham as well; for though he had already fathered Ishmael, it was said: "for in Isaac shall seed be called to you," Ishmael not being legally reckoned his seed (Nedarim 31a); but Abraham our father believed Hashem's promise immediately and rejoiced, leaving no further wonder that Hashem delivered him.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 14:19–20
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: And for this Avraham our Father called the Name of Hashem (Genesis 21:33): 'El Olam' (God of the Universe), demonstrating His glory even within cosmic concealment, akin to what is taught in the Midrash (Kohelet Rabbah 3:11) that 'olam' derives from he'elem (concealment). And Shem was unable to see this, that even in these obscure realms the glory of Heaven abides, therefore he proclaimed the Name of Hashem as 'El Elyon' (God Most High), for Avraham's action in risking his life to rescue Lot was beyond his grasp, and he sought to comprehend it.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Shemot Rabbah 1:1: ‘“These are the names of the children of Israel who came to Egypt with Jacob; each came with his household” (Exodus 1:1). That is what is written: “He who spares his rod hates his son, and he who loves him seeks for him admonition” (Proverbs 13:24). The way of the world is that a person whom another tells him: ‘So-and-so struck your son,’ he would harass him. What is the meaning when the verse states: “He who spares his rod hates his son”? It is to teach you that anyone who withholds rebuke from his son, his son will ultimately set out on a path of depravity and he will hate him. As we find regarding Ishmael, who was beloved by his father Abraham, who did not chasten him, and he set out…’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:47, Rav Tzadok draws upon this midrashic exposition (Shemot Rabbah 1:1) to illuminate his teaching here (“as written in Shemot Rabbah 1:1: that Abraham was the cause in that he spared his rod, therefore Scripture attributed the youth to him; and therefore: “And the thing was very grievous in Abraham's sight”,”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: Only in heavenly judgment does the blessed God incline toward kindness on account of the future. Concerning Moses our teacher, peace be upon him, our sages of blessed memory said that he killed the Egyptian through the explicit Divine Name (Shemot Rabbah, there). In such a case, when he wishes to kill him through heavenly agency, he had to ascertain that no such descendant would emerge, etc.; otherwise, heavenly judgment would not warrant killing him.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: However, the inner meaning is: the primordial light is the supreme bond that unites all worlds together; as explained (regarding Pesach) that at times worlds exist in the aspect of “and one came not near the other” (Exodus 14:20), meaning that they hesitate to channel light to one another lest the recipient be overwhelmed and corrupted by excessive illumination; and at times it is written (Isaiah 6:3): “And one called to the other,” which the Targum renders “and they receive one from another,” where all worlds unite and bestow upon one another.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Genesis 21:11: ‘The matter distressed Abraham greatly, for it concerned a son of his.’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:47, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Genesis 21:11) to illuminate his teaching here (“and therefore: “And the thing was very grievous in Abraham's sight”, meaning that the evil affected his vision—stemming from him and his side, until God said to him: “Let it not be grievous in your sight because of...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And they instituted legal acquisitions to validate agreements, and where ordinary kinyan cannot function they established validity through an oath; through which the matter is ratified, making retraction impossible. And in an Israelite an oath does not effect a property transfer, but places a religious prohibition upon him not to transgress; while for a Noahide there is no religious oath prohibition, acting strictly as a proprietary kinyan where no other acquisition applies; the matter being acquired and ratified through the oath, rendering alteration impossible.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 33:5 (§2)
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: And this is why it is said of him: “and called there on the name of Hashem, the Everlasting God (El Olam)”, which derives from the idiom he'elem (concealment), as brought in the Midrash (Kohelet Rabbah 3:11): “'He has also set the world in their heart'—it is written as concealment”, in that the Ineffable Name was concealed from them; yet even within concealment Avraham radiated heavenly glory in wholeness and called upon Hashem's Name.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Genesis 21:10: ‘She said to Abraham, “Cast out that slave-woman and her son, for the son of that slave shall not share in the inheritance with my son Isaac.”’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:47, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Genesis 21:10) to illuminate his teaching here (“And this is why she said: “with my son, with Isaac”, for Isaac aligns with her spiritual root; unlike Hagar, who also possessed Gevurah to subdue her inclination, having emerged from Egypt that was saturated with lust,”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: So that afterward he begot Yitzchak to be the father of the Israelite nation: "for in Isaac shall your seed be called" (Bereishis 21:12); and Avraham extracts them from Gehinnom, testifying that the sins of those who fell into lust derived merely from the thorns encircling the myrtle (Sanhedrin 44a); but their essential root at birth is circumcised and fenced against true evil.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: Meaning they are uniquely designated “Patriarchs” precisely because no mortal can reach the sublime height of their holiness and service, as we witness that the Blessed Name sealed His holy Name upon them alone, such that we recite (in the Amidah prayer): “God of Abraham, God of Isaac, and God of Jacob”; and this is because no other human being in existence can surrender himself so completely to the Blessed Name as did the Patriarchs.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Bereshit Rabbah 6: ‘“And to rule during the day and at night, and to divide between the light and the darkness, and God saw that it was good” (Genesis 1:18). “And to rule during the day and at night” – Rabbi Ilfa said: If this is referring to the lights, is it not already stated: “The greater light to rule the day”? Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: We begin the book of Genesis immediately after Simchat Torah, even though Nisan is the first of the lunar months, and Israel reckons its calendar according to the moon, as written in Bereishit Rabbah (Parashah 6), so why did they not institute that we begin Genesis after Passover and conclude it on Passover? However, in the Gemara (Rosh Hashanah 11a): according to Rabbi Eliezer that the world was created in Tishrei, in Tishrei they are destined to be redeemed; and according to Rabbi Yehoshua that it was created in Nisan, in Nisan they are destined to be redeemed.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 3:9 (§2)

In the morning he saw the darkness depart and the side of the east light up, he said: Surely over all these there is a Master and Sovereign Ruler Who guides them, etc.”

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Bereshit Rabbah 53:13: ‘“Abraham rose early in the morning, and took bread and a skin of water, and gave them to Hagar, he placed them her shoulder, and the child, and sent her away. It…’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:47, Rav Tzadok draws upon this midrashic exposition (Bereshit Rabbah 53:13) to illuminate his teaching here (“and then Ishmael fell sick Bereishit Rabbah 53:13.”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And likewise it is written: 'a great feast' (mishteh gadol), and it is taught (in Bereishit Rabbah 53): 'The Great One of the worlds was present there'; and that is because the term 'great' (gadol) in the Torah denotes that which is without measure, for otherwise it cannot be termed truly great, since relative to that which is greater than it, it is small; and the expression 'Great One of the worlds' refers to Atika Kadisha.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 1:4–5
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: And as it is written concerning him: "And Avraham rose up early in the morning" (Genesis 22:3), and as brought in the Talmud (Chullin 16a): "Scripture informs us of the fervent alacrity of Avraham." And this is because on high there is neither back of neck (turning away) nor weariness, as taught in the Talmud (Chagigah 15a), and as written concerning the Holy Chayyot (Ezekiel 1:12): "Whithersoever the spirit was to go, they went; they turned not when they went."

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Genesis 21:31: ‘Hence that place was called Beer-sheba, for there the two of them swore an oath.’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:48, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Genesis 21:31) to illuminate his teaching here (“(Genesis 21:31) “Beer-sheba, because there they swore both of them”, Beer-sheba is the border-edge of the Land of Israel, as written: “from Dan even to Beer-sheba”. For there exist the 'scoffer' and the 'simpleton'...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And one must understand, behold we also find in the Torah: "And they drank and became intoxicated with him," (Genesis 43:34), wherein there is mentioned not only the drinking of wine, but actual drunkenness! Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: And that which he answered, “The woman whom You gave to be with me”—means that his defense was that he was compelled to eat; for how was it possible that she should eat while I refrain, leaving her permanently in deficiency with no one to redeem her alongside her lack? And how could he abandon one who had been unified as one essence with him, as taught by the Ari, of blessed memory (Pri Etz Chaim, Sha'ar Rosh Hashanah, ch. 3), that a single wall joined both of them without any dividing partition between them (see above, section 61).

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: II Samuel 24:2: ‘The king said to Joab, his army commander, “Make the rounds of all the tribes of Israel, from Dan to Beer-sheba, and take a census of the people, so that I may know the size of the population.”’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:48, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (II Samuel 24:2) to illuminate his teaching here (“as written: “from Dan even to Beer-sheba”. For there exist the 'scoffer' and the 'simpleton' who represent two opposite extremes, as I heard concerning the homily of our Sages: “Smite a scoffer”—this is Amalek;”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Ref: Ohr Zarua LaTzadik, The Egyptian Exile 5:1 (§2)
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: Therefore they did not know whether he was an Egyptian, for they foresaw that he would be considered an Egyptian as well as a Hebrew. And from this stemmed the error of the king of Egypt, who, seeing that from his domain would emerge the light of the Torah into the world, imagined that it was an ordinary natural product; whereas in truth Moses our teacher, peace be upon him, was from birth and the womb of the seed of Israel and of their holy root and stock, only that through the dedicated effort of Bithiah she merited that he be called her son.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: Fools sin without caution; while the wise discern that judgment is enfolded within the light, conducting themselves with reverent awe. Hence the supreme counsel is to weave the cycles of time together, constricting oneself when the King shines favorably, saving from days of abundance for days of adversity. As Joseph did: “and take up the fifth part of the land of Egypt,” curbing indulgence during abundance lest they perish in famine; instructing them to provide during abundance for the famine to follow.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Proverbs 19:25: ‘Beat scoffers and the simple will become clever;Reprove the intelligent and they gain knowledge.’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:48, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Proverbs 19:25) to illuminate his teaching here (““Smite a scoffer”—this is Amalek; “and the simpleton will learn prudence”—this is Jethro (Tanchuma, Yitro 3): the simpleton believes everything and is filled with devotional cults for everything (and Jethro left...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: For all the words of the Sages derive from Torah and wisdom; when they awaken and illuminate within Jewish hearts some particular teaching of Torah, as a word of Torah enters the heart, the corresponding element of mockery departs against it (Shir HaShirim Rabbah 1:3). And this is the general root power of all the nations, for “the first of the nations is Amalek,” and our Sages of blessed memory expounded (Shemot Rabbah 27): “Strike the scoffer—this is Amalek,” and he is the root and deepest first principle within all the nations.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: And as in Tikkunim (Tikkun 19, 42a): Adam whom the Cause of causes created in His hidden image caused the withdrawal of the Cause of causes; the second Adam sinned in thought, the third Adam sinned in deed; for there are three Adams: Adam of Beriah, Adam of Yetzirah, and Adam of Asiyah. Meaning, to Adam of Asiyah, having become an agent of free choice, the prohibition of the Tree of Knowledge was given, and then Hashem joined the Name Havayah.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Midrash Tanchuma, Yitro 3: ‘Another explanation. You gave to the earliest generations only the fragrance of the commandments. To Adam you gave one commandment, and to Noah and his sons, six commandments, but when we reached Sinai, You poured upon us all the commandments, as men pour ointment from a barrel. Thy name is an ointment (shemen) poured forth. R. Berechiah said: Oil (shemen) is a light to the one who occupies himself with the oil of the Torah. is frequently applied to the Torah. Both are sources of light. R. Berechiah points out that the physical light provided by oil is of no avail without the light of Torah. Therefore do the maidens love thee alludes to the people of the world who come and convert. Who…’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:48, Rav Tzadok draws upon this midrashic exposition (Midrash Tanchuma, Yitro 3) to illuminate his teaching here (““and the simpleton will learn prudence”—this is Jethro (Tanchuma, Yitro 3): the simpleton believes everything and is filled with devotional cults for everything (and Jethro left unserved no idol in the world, etc.),...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: Producing through that intellect cruel decrees of religious persecution and forced assimilation. Persia, however, is titled “simple and unblemished”, which is the antithesis of overt philosophical intellect; not meaning that it lacks intelligence entirely, so as to be deemed simpleton or foolish, but rather that its wisdom remains concealed inwardly, which is the true hallmark of temimut (wholeness/simplicity).
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: And this reflects the difference between the Flood and the Dispersion: as in Tanchuma: The sons of Noah were granted enduring existence; while of the earlier generations it says: “I will make you a terror, and you shall be no more”—as though they never existed. The Flood generation held no enduring being, vanishing as though never created, made only for a transient hour; while the Dispersion already possessed enduring being, yet having stubbornly weaponized the guise of unity to force the divine Will to dwell amidst their sins —.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Mekhilta d'Rabbi Yishmael 18:11: “‘Now I know that the Lord is greater than all the gods’ (Exodus 18:11): They said concerning Jethro that he did not leave a single idol in the world without worshiping it and investigating its cult, and therefore his testimony recognizing the sovereignty of Hashem carried unique weight.” Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:48, Rav Tzadok draws upon this midrashic exposition (Mekhilta d'Rabbi Yishmael 18:11) to illuminate his teaching here (“(and Jethro left unserved no idol in the world, etc.), while the scoffer believes nothing and serves nothing at all. And always the middle path is the line of integrity, yet there is also an extreme edge of holiness...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And all the more so did they guard their eyes from gazing upon forbidden sights; yet because Ahasuerus gave thanks to his gods, there adhered a taint of idolatry matching the desire of Haman; and following the path of Haman of the seed of Esav: displaying split hooves, judging merely by superficial appearances rather than the inward heart!
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: As in Menachot (110a): that they call Him “the God of gods.” Hence idolatry is termed dachla (fear/dread), seeking an abstract dread to free themselves to act according to the malice of their hearts. As said of the Egyptians regarding their deity: “their dread,” worshiping the lamb; because they enjoyed material bounty in immense abundance, which the lamb represents, as in Chullin (84b): Why are flocks called ashtarot? Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And our father Abraham, peace be upon him, head of the Jewish nation, his star is the brilliant luminary appearing each night first among the stars adjacent to the moon, shining with great intensity as is known, and that star they named Jupiter (Tzedek, Righteousness) [after Abraham, expounded in Bereishit Rabbah 49 on "You loved righteousness (tzedek)," as well as "Who raised up righteousness (tzedek) from the east," calling Abraham Tzedek, after whom his star was named; for "He counts the number of the stars, He calls them all by names," naming each according to the spiritual radiance of the Jewish soul corresponding to it, which only Hashem can name].

And this is what is written: “And for man there was not found a helper opposite him”; for when inanimate, vegetable, and animal entities enter man and he elevates them, subsumed into his being.

Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: Its secret is known [as expounded] in Tikkunei Zohar Chadash and in the sefer Arba Me’os Shekel Kesef of the Arizal.: the “secret” of yedi’ah (Divine knowledge) and bechirah (free choice) is expounded in the Kabbalah — in Tikkunei Zohar Chadash, and in Arba Me’os Shekel Kesef, a work of the Arizal’s Kabbalah (its title drawn from “four hundred silver shekels,” Bereishis 23:16). There the two are set on different planes of the supernal roots: from the side of God’s knowledge (the higher unity) there is no independent “choice,” while free choice belongs to the “place” of this lower world — so that the two do not contradict.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 11:7
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: Indeed, even within eternal life there exist manifold degrees, what demonstrates this? That even his beloved only son, given to him at one hundred years, he served Hashem even within this salvation of eternal life, and offered him as an elevation offering unto Hashem, hoping and yearning unto Hashem to reach the ultimate purpose and root of all things, and as Hashem testified concerning him (Genesis 26:5): “Because Avraham obeyed My voice”, specifically 'My voice' extending to the Infinite.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Yevamot 63a: ‘And Rabbi Elazar said: What is the meaning of that which is written: “This is now bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh” (Genesis 2:23)? This teaches that Adam had intercourse with each animal and beast in his search for his mate, and his mind was not at ease, in accordance with the verse: “And for Adam, there was not found a helpmate for him” (Genesis 2:20), until he had intercourse with Eve.’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:50, Rav Tzadok draws upon this talmudic and halakhic source (Yevamot 63a) to illuminate his teaching here (“as written in Yevamot 63a. And because perfection consists of integrating both attributes, which is why an unmarried man is half a body Zohar III 7b; and nonetheless each one individually must be integrated within both,”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And this was the deep sleep of Adam in Bereishit Rabbah (18:4) on "This is now" Genesis 2:23: she agitated him all night, appearing in his dream; for when all animals passed before Adam he longed for a mate and his mind was not set at ease (Yevamot 63a), and from unfulfilled yearning he grew weary and fell asleep; his sleep filled with dreams, and being initially two-faced back-to-back (Berakhot 61a) sharing one life, when he slept and conscious wisdom withdrew, it was transferred into her.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: Meaning, where the soul once dwelt, it will certainly not allow it to be said of it that it resided in an unworthy inn; and therefore the soul will willingly humble itself to descend back into the body to revive it. And this is: “And the man said: This time it is bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh; she shall be called Woman, because she was taken out of Man” (Genesis 2:23).

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Zohar, Vayikra 13:97-16:104: ‘The verse continues: “It is like the precious oil upon the head that ran down upon the beard.” This is the oil of the anointing of holiness which streams forth from the Ancient Holy One and which is found in that supernal stream which gives to the children the wherewithal to kindle the lights. That oil trickles on to the head of the King and from the head to the holy and venerable beard, and from there it streams on to all the garments of splendour in which the King is arrayed, as it is written, “that came down upon the skirt of his garments”. These are the Crowns of the King in which is found the Holy Name:’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:50, Rav Tzadok draws upon this kabbalistic teaching (Zohar, Vayikra 13:97-16:104) to illuminate his teaching here (“which is why an unmarried man is half a body Zohar III 7b; and nonetheless each one individually must be integrated within both, and for this purpose unfolded all the trials of Abraham as I wrote above in sections...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And then she captured the light: she gave to her husband as noted above (having been taken from man), so that within the man's bestowal to another in this passion there was likewise conceived the knowledge of evil, tainting human generation at its root in the sense of "in iniquity was I brought forth". And the kelipah seized that light: the divine influx intended for the holy Eshet Chayil to channel in purity was siphoned into this root of self-serving knowledge of evil; whence the dark realm was filled from the ruin of the Eshet Chayil, configuring a complete counter-stature with its four worlds of Atzilut, Beriah, Yetzirah, and Asiyah.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: “And he sent forth a raven, which went forth to and fro, until the waters were dried up from off the earth.” My revered father explained in Mei HaShiloach: the raven symbolizes anger, and Noah sought through this to banish the attribute of anger completely from the world. And the term “vayeshallach” (he banished/sent away) indicates this intention, as in Zohar Acharei Mot (72a) on Genesis 38:17: “I will send a kid from the flock” — a parable of a king with a son from a maidservant roaming his palace; wherefore it is written not “I will give” but “I will send”—banishing him so he be found in the palace no more.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Genesis 25:19: ‘This is the story of Isaac, son of Abraham. Abraham begot Isaac.’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:50, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Genesis 25:19) to illuminate his teaching here (“and this is: “These are the generations of Isaac, Abraham's son: Abraham begot Isaac”, behold holy awe born directly from love, and he inherently possessed the attribute of love by birth, for “a son is the leg of his...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: Therefore, from the side of Israel’s servitude, which is the arousal from below, fear comes first; but from the side of His middos, it is known that love precedes, as it says, “Yours, Hashem, is the greatness [gedulah] and the might [gevurah]” — greatness first; and so among the Avos, who are the Chariot, “Avraham begot Yitzchak.”
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: The fourth, “And God divided between the light [and the darkness],” corresponds to nursing/weaning, and to Isaac our Father, who possessed resolute fortitude that whatever he performed was good (as explained in Parashat Lech Lecha, section 17). And the fifth, “And God called the light Day,” corresponds to mature consciousness (mochin), and to Jacob our Father—an unbounded heritage—empowered to engender ongoing generations.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Eruvin 70b: ‘Or perhaps an heir is like his father’s foot, i.e., he is considered an extension of his father and substitutes for him in all regards, which means that just as his father could have renounced his rights, so can he. Rav Naḥman said to him: I myself say that an heir can indeed renounce rights in a courtyard, while those scholars of the school of Shmuel taught: He cannot renounce rights in a courtyard. Rava raised an objection to Rav Naḥman from the following baraita: This is the principle: Anything that is permitted for part of Shabbat is permitted for all of Shabbat, and anything that is prohibited for part of Shabbat is prohibited for all of Shabbat, apart from one who renounces his…’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:50, Rav Tzadok draws upon this talmudic and halakhic source (Eruvin 70b) to illuminate his teaching here (“for “a son is the leg of his father” Eruvin 70b; and the Binding of Isaac itself—the yearning of the soul unto Hashem— was rooted in love, as it is written: “My soul yearns, yea, even faints for the courts of Hashem.””), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: Unlike human souls which are in the divine image, encompassing all cosmic faculties, as Scripture titled them (Deuteronomy 14:1): "You are children to Hashem your God," and a son is the leg of his father, as stated in Eruvin (70b); meaning, because a father endows his son with five attributes (Eduyot 2:9), which encompass all potential aspects of perfection, though nevertheless he is not as complete as the father himself, but in the ratio and proportion of the leg to the whole body.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: And separation indicates that the transcendent realm is completely set apart from mortal reach; for man cannot legitimately penetrate what lies beyond the boundary of his intellect; only within the perimeter of his conscious grasp has God permitted him to walk, serving his Creator through discernment, discipline, and refined character traits; whereas if he attempts to trespass into what lies beyond his designated pale, he will be utterly destroyed.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Psalms 84:3: ‘I long, I yearn for the courts of the ETERNAL One;my body and soul shout for joy to the living God.’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:50, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Psalms 84:3) to illuminate his teaching here (“as it is written: “My soul yearns, yea, even faints for the courts of Hashem.” And Scripture testified of Sarah Bereishit Rabbah 58:1: at one hundred she was like twenty regarding sin—in that she did not sin, from...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And when one is literally "with all your soul," offering his life at the moment of the act, it is "my soul pined" (Psalms 84:3)—literal expiration of the soul, matching Ketubot (62b): her heart failed and her spirit fled, the ultimate state of being "lovesick" (Song of Songs 2:5). Yet "in the light of the King's countenance is life" (Proverbs 16:15), so that actual death is averted by the King's countenance shining upon him as the Source of Life, instantly replenishing him with new life through that self-sacrifice.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: As in Midrash Tehillim (82): The soul seeks every hour to depart the body, so how does it remain? Hashem's glory fills the earth, and as the soul rushes to depart it beholds its Maker within the world and steps back into the body. Meaning, the soul yearns to return to its quarry, but when Hashem reveals that His glory fills all creation, it willingly abides here, discerning that it is far more precious to magnify His glory in this lowly world where light is hidden and darkness reigns.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Bereshit Rabbah 58:1: ‘“Sarah’s lifetime was one hundred years and twenty years and seven years, the years of the life of Sarah” (Genesis 23:1). “Sarah’s lifetime was one hundred years.” “The Lord knows the days of the faultless; their inheritance will last forever” (Psalms 37:18) – just as they are faultless, so their years are faultless: When twenty years old she was like a seven year old girl regarding beauty, and when a hundred years old she was like a twenty year old regarding sin. Another matter, “the Lord knows the days of the faultless [temimim]” – this refers to Sarah, who was faultless in her actions. Rabbi Yoḥanan said: Like a calf without blemish [temima]. “Their inheritance will last forever,” as…’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:50, Rav Tzadok draws upon this midrashic exposition (Bereshit Rabbah 58:1) to illuminate his teaching here (“And Scripture testified of Sarah Bereishit Rabbah 58:1: at one hundred she was like twenty regarding sin—in that she did not sin, from the essence of her own attribute Gevurah, as is known from our Sages that awe is...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And regarding the phrase "the sons of Seir who settled the land," on which the Talmud asked in Shabbat [85a]: "Did the rest of humanity dwell in the sky?", the plain meaning denotes the sovereign masters of the soil prior to the arrival of Esau, parallel to Bereishit Rabbah [58] on "and Ephron sat/dwelled"—that he was appointed governor that day, since true "dwelling" implies mastery and presiding at the helm.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: “And the Lord said: My spirit shall not abide in man forever, for that he also is flesh; therefore shall his days be a hundred and twenty years.” It is stated in Tractate Chullin (139b): Where is Moses alluded to in the Torah? In the verse: “For that he also (be-shagam = 345 = Moshe) is flesh”; and it is necessary to understand: What was the Gemara's question? Is it a small matter that Moses is mentioned countless times throughout the Torah?

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Genesis 23:9: ‘Let him sell me the cave of Machpelah that he owns, which is at the edge of his land. Let him sell it to me, at the full price, for a burial site in your midst.”’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:51, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Genesis 23:9) to illuminate his teaching here (“(Genesis 23:9) “the cave of Machpelah, which he has, which is in the end of his field”, for Kiriath-arba (City of Four)—who are Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and Adam— is Hebron, meaning: the union (chibur) of all souls”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Ref: Ohr Zarua LaTzadik, Novellae, Rambam, Melachim 10:4
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And according to this is resolved the objection of Ner Tamid [Keritot 10b], who wrote: – According to Rabbeinu Tam who distinguishes between Adam and ha-Adam, the question of Tosafot in Bava Batra 58a returns: why did Rabbi Banna'ah mark the cave of Abraham, when graves of gentiles do not transmit ritual impurity?! – And what was answered that Abraham is called Adam because it is written "the great man (ha-adam ha-gadol)" [Joshua 14:15] does not apply to Rabbeinu Tam, for according to him ha-adam includes gentiles!
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: As found in the mitzvah of Shemitah: wherein man constricts himself one year out of every seven, eating his harvest with measured pauses rather than consuming all at once, thereby retaining his land forever. And when they violated this mitzvah they incurred seventy years of exile corresponding to the neglected Shemitah years, as written (Leviticus 26:34): “Then shall the land enjoy her sabbaths”; which operated not as vindictive punishment, but from their own doing: refusing pauses in receiving bounty and eating continuously, they had to absorb all sabbatical pauses at once, the land turning desolate as they were exiled.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Jerusalem Talmud Avodah Zarah 3:1: ‘9:1 (Notes 56–58). Rebbi Zeˋira the son of Rebbi Abbahu preached before Rebbi Eleazar. Happy is he whom the God of Jacob helps. 146:5–6.. What is written after this? The Maker of Heaven and Earth. What has one to do with the other? But a king of flesh and blood needs a protector “protector, defender”.; in one district he is not a ruler, maybe in another one? If you say a universal ruler rules over dry land, does he [rule] over the Sea? But the Holy One, praise to Him, is not like this; He rules over the Sea, He rules over dry land. Not only this, but if a sword is at a person’s neck the Holy One, praise to Him, saves him. That is what Moses said, He saved me from Pharao’ s sword. 18:4..…’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:51, Rav Tzadok draws upon this talmudic and halakhic source (Jerusalem Talmud Avodah Zarah 3:1) to illuminate his teaching here (“as written in Yerushalmi Avodah Zarah (3:1), and in a sphere the beginning and the end meet at one single point; and thus Adam and the Messiah, namely David, are all one. And the union of all four, which is the...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: But regarding Rabbi Abbahu, they related in the Yerushalmi [Avodah Zarah 3:1] that before his passing they showed him thirteen rivers of pure balsam oil, whereupon he exclaimed: "Then I said: I have labored in vain (l'rik yagati)!" (Yeshayah 49:4); and it is known [from the Kavvanos of the Ari] on the prayer "that we may not labor in vain (la-rik)" that rik has the letters of keri, for such is, God forbid, the toil of the flesh in vain; and likewise they expounded on "nor bring forth for terror" (Yeshayah 65:23): this refers to spirits, demons, and lilin.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 33:9
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: “Maker/Possessor of heaven and earth”—as we recite “King of the Universe”, this being the blessing recited before all pleasures, to ensure the bounty does not harm human intellect, since the King desires the welfare of His people. And this is “Maker of heaven and earth”— meaning Hashem renews and rectifies them continually, as brought in the holy Zohar (Vayigash 207a): “'He established the heavens by understanding'—what is 'established'?

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Bava Batra 58a: ‘When he arrived at the cave of Adam the first man, who is buried in the same area, a Divine Voice emerged and said: You gazed upon the likeness of My image, i.e., Abraham, who is similar to the image of Adam the first man. Do not gaze upon My image itself, i.e., Adam the first man, about whom the verse states that he was formed in the image of God (see Genesis 1:27). Rabbi Bena’a said: But I need to mark the cave. The voice said to him: As the measurements of the dimensions of the outer cave where Abraham is buried, so are the measurements of the dimensions of the inner cave, where Adam is buried. The Gemara notes: And according to the one who says that the Cave of Machpelah consists of…’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:51, Rav Tzadok draws upon this talmudic and halakhic source (Bava Batra 58a) to illuminate his teaching here (“as our Sages noted (Bava Batra 58a): just as the upper story is the choicest of his possessions and rides above the house, like soul upon body; so in the lower house reside the separated bodies,”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: Yet one must consider Rabbi Bena'ah in Bava Batra 58a who relied on behavioral assessment to identify brazen sons as illegitimate for inheritance, though in monetary matters we do not follow a presumption to extract money; except that there nine were definitely illegitimate, whereas here who says either is a mamzer; and furthermore, the father instructed that only the true son inherit, entrusting the court to discern the heir through their wisdom; resembling Ketubot 85b ("my estate to Tuvia") where the court exercises judicial discretion (shuda dedayane) according to Rashi to assess the testator's intent.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: And this is the Zohar: “‘Let there be light’—from Chochmah; ‘and there was light’—from Binah.” And further: “‘Let us make man in our image’—that is the light; ‘after our likeness’—that is the darkness which serves as a garment to the light, etc.” Therefore concerning all creations it is written “and it was so,” while concerning light it is written “and there was light”: for “and it was so” denotes that creation emerged exactly as the utterance itself, the utterance expanding until it was realized, the entity becoming the direct embodiment of the speech (see section 6).

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Gittin 68b: ‘Ashmedai said to him: Take the chain engraved with God’s name off me and give me your ring with God’s name engraved on it, and I will show you my strength. Solomon took the chain off him and he gave him his ring. Ashmedai swallowed the ring and grew until he placed one wing in the heaven and one wing on the earth. He threw Solomon a distance of four hundred parasangs. With regard to that moment Solomon said: “What profit is there for a person through all of his toil under the sun?” (Ecclesiastes 1:3). With Solomon deposed from the throne, Ashmedai took his place.’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:51, Rav Tzadok draws upon this talmudic and halakhic source (Gittin 68b) to illuminate his teaching here (“and as Ashmedai said in the chapter Mi SheAchazo (Gittin 68b): he measured four cubits of earth, etc.; and in Tamid (32b) concerning Alexander the Great with the eyeball, that a handful of dust covers the covetous eye”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And in himself he was secure as noted above, whereas regarding his throne—which corresponds to the World of Creation (Beriah), situated outside Hashem's transcendent essence— there external forces can gain dominion, requiring the seal wherewith the Holy One sealed His world as mentioned above]. And this signet-ring constituted all of Solomon's strength, and through it he returned to his kingdom as recounted in chapter Mi SheAchazo (Gittin 68b).
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: Until he re-attains that very same illumination he possessed before entering the world—which is the summit of human perfection. And concerning this Scripture hints (Ecclesiastes 4:15): “I saw all the living who walk under the sun, with the second child”; and “the second child” alludes to this light which man acquires for himself through toil, following the concealment of the first light he experienced in the womb.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Tamid 32b: ‘He said to the Sages: What is this? Why does this eyeball outweigh everything?
