The Sages answered him: Take a small amount of dirt and cover the eye. He did so, and it was immediately balanced by its proper counterweight. The eye is never satisfied while it can see, as it is written: “The netherworld and destruction are never satiated; so the eyes of man are never satiated” (Proverbs 27:20).’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:51, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Tamid 32b) to illuminate his teaching here (“and in Tamid (32b) concerning Alexander the Great with the eyeball, that a handful of dust covers the covetous eye which is never satisfied with any pleasure, and outweighs all gold, see there. Therefore, this burial...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And Moses our teacher, peace be upon him, did not conduct himself according to standard derekh eretz regarding marital intimacy, which is likewise termed derekh eretz, and therefore Aaron and Miriam spoke against him on this account, considering him to have neglected a mitzvah since his wife had not explicitly waived her marital rights; and certainly, since it was recorded in the Torah, their words contained some substance as well.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: Meaning, although the Blessed Name created the sea as well, nevertheless from the perspective of mortals His glory is not discernible there, for in the sea the human form has no stable footing to expand; as stated in the Gemara (Tamid 32a) that all who go down to the sea have their minds unsettled, and therefore man from his vantage point perceives no overt Heavenly glory there.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Bava Metzia 87a: ‘From where do we derive this principle that the wicked say much and do not do even a little? We derive it from Ephron. Initially, it is written that Ephron said to Abraham: “A piece of land worth four hundred shekels of silver, what is that between me and you?” (Genesis 23:15). And ultimately it is written: “And Abraham listened to Ephron; and Abraham weighed to Ephron the silver, which he had named in the hearing of the children of Heth, four hundred shekels of silver, current money with the merchant” (Genesis 23:16), i.e., shekels that could be used in any location. This teaches that not only did Ephron take shekels from Abraham, he took from him only centenaria [kantarei], i.e.,…’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:51, Rav Tzadok draws upon this talmudic and halakhic source (Bava Metzia 87a) to illuminate his teaching here (“who was the evil-eyed one as our Sages noted (Bava Metzia 87a) (and so it is in gematria: “ra ayin” = 400), he being evil-eyed and never satisfied with little; and this exists for him at the end of his field,”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And such was the genesis of evil in the world, the root of evil seeking expansion, whereas it must remain contracted as a single point ("if one is full the other is desolate", which is Rome built then)]. And from her issued Nebuchadnezzar, whom the Holy One designated "My servant", as our Sages taught in Sanhedrin: "A servant who acquired possessions...", operating in the mystery of Solomon's servants [and as our Sages noted: Solomon is named after the Name of the Holy One, meaning he sought to expand Hashem's power through concealed depths where division does not exist.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: Man becomes aware that he possesses moral free will, empowered consciously to reject evil and choose good. And this is what they answered: “To exact retribution from the wicked...” — for initially, before creation had endured suffering, sinning touched only the realm between man and God; and before the Almighty sin blemish was as nothing, the destroyer of a world having ruined no human investment.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Genesis 23:16: ‘Abraham accepted Ephron’s terms. Abraham paid out to Ephron the money that he had named in the hearing of the Hittites—four hundred shekels of silver at the going merchants’ rate.’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:51, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Genesis 23:16) to illuminate his teaching here (“(and so it is in gematria: “ra ayin” = 400), he being evil-eyed and never satisfied with little; and this exists for him at the end of his field, and when a person eventually dies they show him burial which points to...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: Even though in truth through hearing directly they would have merited eternal life; this being the first onset of sin born of this world of falsehood which portrays everything in reverse of the truth; so that in place of authentic life they experienced the terror of death; and although from the perspective of this earthly world it was indeed death; for it would have been the death of mortal bodily life, meriting the ultimate rectification of entering Gan Eden alive, the true dwelling of Man.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: And this was renewed after the Flood: through rebuke the foundations were strengthened with awe, never to expand lawlessly again. Whereby creation secured absolute acquisition, as words backed by monetary payment—the immense blood and suffering paid by the world. Therefore retracting on words backed by money incurs the curse of the Flood: “He who took retribution from the Generation of the Flood will take retribution from him who stands not by his word,” because he undermines the fabric of reality, treating paid transactions as revocable, deserving retribution to re-solidify the bond.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Sotah 34b: ‘The Gemara asks: But is the land in Hebron in fact stony? But isn’t it written: “And it came to pass at the end of forty years, that Absalom said to the king: I pray, let me go and pay my vow, which I have vowed to the Lord, in Hebron” (II Samuel 15:7)? And Rav Avya says, and some say that it was Rabba bar bar Ḥanan: This means that Absalom went to bring sheep specifically from Hebron. And it is taught in a baraita (Tosefta, Menaḥot 9:3): One must bring the choicest animals to the Temple as offerings. Rams are brought from Moab, and sheep are brought from Hebron. This indicates that Hebron has rich land where fat and healthy sheep are raised. The Gemara answers: From this very source it…’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:51, Rav Tzadok draws upon this talmudic and halakhic source (Sotah 34b) to illuminate his teaching here (“Therefore they said in Sotah (34b): that Hebron is rocky soil, which is why it was chosen for burial, meaning: it does not yield worldly physical delights; and they stated there: at any rate sheep come from Hebron...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Ref: Likkutei Maamarim, On Book of Joshua:16 (§5)
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: Therefore Moses added to him the letter Yud, representing divine Thought and Supernal Wisdom, meaning that his intellect be shielded by Hashem: "May God (Yah) save you from the counsel of the spies." And with this Name (Yah) the Sages taught that this world and the World to Come were created (Menachot 29b), so that the intent of this Name is the harmonization of both worlds; denoting the perception of the World to Come within this world, which is the essence of inheriting the Land and the Oral Torah: recognizing in physical affairs that nothing is truly detached from Hashem.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: And all prayer must be directed toward that supernal point to be self-nullified there, for there is the inception of being, as written (I Kings 8:48): “and pray unto You toward their land”; because when man purifies his heart and reaches that source, he can transform evil into good, for there absolute unity reigns, where no change exists in the Creator’s Will.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Ezekiel 34:31: ‘For you—My flock, the flock that I tend—are human; and I am your God—declares the Sovereign GOD.’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:51, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Ezekiel 34:31) to illuminate his teaching here (“for the flock of their pasture: “you are men”. Therefore King David, peace be upon him, the faithful shepherd, was anointed king over all Israel in Hebron—the place of pasture; and also because there lies the union...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And God made man upright (Koheles 7:29): for on the contrary, the bitterness of the gallbladder sweetens the liver when functioning properly, casting merely a single droplet to calm its fury; unlike when it overflows through the dominance of the evil forces within the turbid blood of the liver and the sword of the Angel of Death residing within the bile (Avodah Zarah 20b); and all sins are attributed to the Nefesh, as it is said: "If a soul (nefesh) shall sin" (Vayikra 4:2); for there is the empowerment of the animal soul—the soul-level of the nations who are not termed "Adam"—which enclothes and encircles the soul of man in an Israelite.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 1:5–6
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: Just as we observe that all organs of a human being submit beneath his intellect to sense instantly the thoughts and sovereign will of the person, such that even the toes of his feet felt the desire formulated in the brain to walk unto this specific destination that arises in his thought. And this corresponds to what is taught in the Midrash (Bereishit Rabbah 39:1): that Avraham our Father saw a burning/illuminated palace, and wondered: "Can it be that this palace is without a governor?"

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Avodah Zarah 5a: ‘The Gemara answers: Do not say that if our ancestors had not sinned we would not have come into the world, as we still would have been born; rather, it would have been as though we had not come into the world. We would have been of no importance, due to the previous generations that would have still been alive. The Gemara asks: Is this to say that if the Jewish people had not sinned with the Golden Calf then they would not have died? But isn’t the chapter that addresses widows whose husbands die childless (Deuteronomy 25:5–10) written in the Torah, and the chapter that addresses the inheritance a deceased father bequeaths to his sons (Numbers 27:8–11) is also written?’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:51, Rav Tzadok draws upon this talmudic and halakhic source (Avodah Zarah 5a) to illuminate his teaching here (“and in the manner that they said in Avodah Zarah 5a: “Come, let us give thanks to our ancestors, for had they not died, we would not have been born”, see there; and physical death is the absence of eternal physical...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: To the extent that they said in Avodah Zarah 5a: were it not that our ancestors sinned, we would be as those who never needed to be born into this world, for they would never have died at all. For true vitality is eternal life, and not a momentary existence "for a brief flash" like the life of this world. And our father Jacob, peace be upon him, who is the root of the attribute of truth, certainly merited this; and even while he was still clothed in the physical garment of this world.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: In that moment this consciousness was born in man, falling into dread lest he possessed independent power to rebel, causing his trembling. Therefore it asks where Haman is alluded to—where it is hinted that Israel could fall into such darkness, fearing God had abandoned them; resolving from “Hamin ha-etz” and “haster astir” — meaning that when Hashem rebuked Adam, he experienced dread greater than Haman's era, Hashem rebuking him as though his eating had not been ordained.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Genesis 23:16: ‘Abraham accepted Ephron’s terms. Abraham paid out to Ephron the money that he had named in the hearing of the Hittites—four hundred shekels of silver at the going merchants’ rate.’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:51, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Genesis 23:16) to illuminate his teaching here (“And he paid its price: “four hundred shekels of silver”, corresponding to Kiriath-arba (the City of Four), as I have written elsewhere, that the number 400 everywhere in the words of our Sages,”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: Therefore at Sinai Israel proclaimed "we will do and we will hear," meriting the higher rung of "hearing," achieving complete liberation from the evil inclination, the Angel of Death, and foreign subjugation (Avodah Zarah 5a); through absolute divine oneness, wherein all opposing forces and impediments dissolve, for in pure unity no division can exist.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: Afterward Hashem seals His covenant upon Israel as possessing permanent integration, bestowing the Holy Temple—His seal in this world—manifesting that communion of disparate elements is real even in this corporeal realm. Therefore it was built on high in the Land of Israel (highest of lands), upon the Temple Mount in Jerusalem, because the integration radiating in the Sanctuary is accepted voluntarily by Israel, held not with stubborn coercion; knowing there is no coercion without Hashem's Will, seeking only to recognize that He sanctifies them in every individual action.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Genesis 24:1: ‘Abraham was now old, advanced in years, and GOD had blessed Abraham in all things.’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:52, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Genesis 24:1) to illuminate his teaching here (“Genesis 24:1 “And Abraham was old”, old age derives from toil, as written in Kiddushin 33a: how many hardships and adventures passed over this elder, etc.,”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: This "head of gold" denoting Nebuchadnezzar, who in the unholy husk stands opposite King David in holiness; as written on "as is the good"—this is David; "as is the sinner"—this is Nebuchadnezzar; the one built the Temple and reigned forty years, while the other destroyed it and reigned forty years. And the number forty corresponds to the twenty-eight attributes (Ko'ach) of David, each comprising ten; representing the three intellectual faculties (Mochin) of the Skull and the Surrounding Light.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: And within this tree lay goodness, but indistinguishable from evil. Indeed, in other trees imperfection was also present—one good for food but plain in appearance, another beautiful but lesser in taste; showing that individual perfection was lacking, yet in them good and evil were readily discernible. And the twenty generations from Adam to Abraham correspond to the Davidic monarchy, David mirroring Adam; and David received the choicest of his years: the thirty years of the tenth century being the pinnacle of Adam's life.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Kiddushin 33a: ‘Before the hoary head of an elder you shall stand and revere; you shall stand and revere the face of an elder. From the fact that the Merciful One did not write this and thereby divide the two concepts, learn from it that “elder” and “hoary head” are together referring to one type of person. The Master said previously in the baraita: One might have thought that he should revere him through money, i.e., he is required to give him money in his honor; therefore, the verse states: “You shall stand and you shall revere” (Leviticus 19:32). Just as standing includes no monetary loss, so too, reverence is referring to an action that includes no monetary loss. The Gemara asks: And does standing…’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:52, Rav Tzadok draws upon this talmudic and halakhic source (Kiddushin 33a) to illuminate his teaching here (“as written in Kiddushin 33a: how many hardships and adventures passed over this elder, etc., and as written in Eruvin 22a: the steep ascents and descents aged them,”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: While "hoary head" (seivah) likewise denotes a sage, yet he is not termed an "elder" (zaken) because the Torah has not yet become his integrated acquisition], and such students are not yet of the stature of a "great man" (gavra rabba) empowered to authoritatively deduct lashes from the biblical text, nor has the Torah become their personal acquisition.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: Ar'ekka related to yir'ah (awe): I Myself shall be your living awe as though standing directly before your face; the fear of Hashem standing before you continually, never subordinating yourself to an astrological intermediary for passive awe; rather, only after man advances on his part through rigorous clarifications—exercising free choice, awe, integration, and selflessness through conscious calculation — only afterward does Hashem seal His Name upon that soul, that permanent sanctity now abides within him even below conscious thought.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Eruvin 22a: ‘And that is what Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said: What is the meaning of that which is written: “And you shall keep the commandments, and the statutes, and the judgments which I command you today to do them” (Deuteronomy 7:11)? It means: Today is the time to do them, in this world, and tomorrow is not the time to do them, as there is no obligation or opportunity to fulfill mitzvot in the World-to-Come. Furthermore, it means: Today is the time to do them, but only tomorrow, in the ultimate future, is the time to receive reward for doing them.’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:52, Rav Tzadok draws upon this talmudic and halakhic source (Eruvin 22a) to illuminate his teaching here (“and as written in Eruvin 22a: the steep ascents and descents aged them, and likewise in the days of man there are ascents and descents throughout his lifetime, over which all human toil and divine labor unfold,”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: Yet the Sages concluded in Berakhot (17a): The ultimate purpose of wisdom is repentance and good deeds; this being the overarching goal in this world: actualizing the divine will in physical deed, wherefore the mitzvot require action. And this is the whole Torah: instructing deed; as written in Menachot (29b): this world created with Heh (action) and the World to Come with Yud (thought), the letter Heh signifying deed in the Zohar, this being the core of this world: "this day to do them, and tomorrow to receive their reward" Eruvin 22a.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 5:8
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: The concept is: the conduct of this world and Hashem's bestowal in this world is in the mystery of 'Tzedek' (Righteousness / natural order), meaning through good laws embedded naturally within man and his habituation to them as an ingrained decree without conscious reflection. For as for knowing that 'I am Hashem Who sanctifies you', this Hashem stores up for the upright in the ultimate future, and then Hashem will unveil and open man's reward and deed to repay him according to his labor of serving with a whole heart in conscious understanding.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Bereshit Rabbah 29:3: ‘Rabbi Simon said: The Holy One blessed be He found three [precious] finds: Abraham, as it is written: “You found his heart faithful before You” (Nehemiah 9:8); David, as it is written: “I found David, My servant” (Psalms 89:21); Israel, as it is written: “Like grapes in the wilderness I found Israel” (Hosea 9:10). The students raised an objection to Rabbi Simon: But is it not written [also]: “But Noah found favor”? He said to them: He [Noah] found [favor], the Holy One blessed be He did not find [him]. But is it not written: “[Israel] found favor in the wilderness”? (Jeremiah 31:2). It is due to the merit of the generation of the Wilderness. (“You found his heart faithful before You.”)).’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:52, Rav Tzadok draws upon this midrashic exposition (Bereshit Rabbah 29:3) to illuminate his teaching here (“And our Sages of blessed memory noted Bereishit Rabbah 29:3: three notable finds did the Holy One encounter: in Abraham, Israel, and David and facing them is that which is stated in Berakhot 5a:”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And surely this reservation applies not only to 'you labored and did not find,' for the divine measure of reward is far greater than punishment, and if it is possible to labor and not find, all the more so is it possible that without prior labor one finds through Heavenly assistance, and along the lines of "And Noah found grace in the eyes of Hashem" (Genesis 6:8), concerning which our Sages expounded (Bereishit Rabbah 29:1): he found grace, but the Holy One, blessed be He, did not find grace in him.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 3:3
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: "Unto the land that I will show you"— meaning that the Generation of the Dispersion knew that Hashem does not desire the destruction of the world, for from Creation onward He desires its enduring existence, even if the world is not deserving, as brought in the Midrash (Bereishit Rabbah 29:1): “'And Noach found grace'—even Noach was not inherently worthy, except that he found grace”; therefore when Hashem brought the waters of the Flood upon the earth He preserved Noach and his sons from whom the world was rebuilt, not desiring universal destruction.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Berakhot 5a: ‘And Rabbi Levi bar Ḥama said that Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish said: God said to Moses, “Ascend to Me on the mountain and be there, and I will give you the stone tablets and the Torah and the mitzva that I have written that you may teach them” (Exodus 24:12), meaning that God revealed to Moses not only the Written Torah, but all of Torah, as it would be transmitted through the generations. The “tablets” are the ten commandments that were written on the tablets of the Covenant, the “Torah” is the five books of Moses. The “mitzva” is the Mishna, which includes explanations for the mitzvot and how they are to be performed. “That I have written” refers to the Prophets and Writings, written with…’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:52, Rav Tzadok draws upon this talmudic and halakhic source (Berakhot 5a) to illuminate his teaching here (“and facing them is that which is stated in Berakhot 5a: three precious gifts: Torah, the Land of Israel, and the World to Come, as I have written elsewhere;”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: But “the eye sees,” so that through it “the heart covets” — [and] these are soul-powers drawn from the neshamah. And even though the essential “seeing” of the soul is in purity and holiness of sight — to see only “visions of God” even in every physical thing of this world, this “sight” being drawn from “fear [yirah],” the rung of “Aryeh” [whose “letters are the letters of yirah”], the root of the holiness of Knesses Yisrael, the “gathering” of the souls of Israel — nonetheless, by virtue of the bond of the material body — which is the “feet,” through which “man rules over man to his detriment” — [the evil] rules also over the faculty of “sight,” making it…
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: Attributing the parting of waters to the Ark rather than the Tablets, the Tablets embodying internal light (positive mitzvot) and the Ark embodying surrounding light (negative mitzvot). So with Joseph's coffin in Yalkut Shimoni: “‘The sea saw it, and fled’—what did it see? It saw the coffin of Joseph descending into the sea”; attributing the sea's flight to the coffin rather than Joseph within, the coffin being surrounding light; because Joseph embodied the covenant of constriction, withdrawing from Potiphar’s wife.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Jeremiah 17:9: ‘Most devious is the heart;It is perverse—who can fathom it?’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:52, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Jeremiah 17:9) to illuminate his teaching here (“as it is stated: “The heart is deceitful above all things, and incurably sick”; and there reside the good and evil inclinations: “A wise man's heart, etc.”. However, the very inception of primal thought—is from...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And this is termed the "mystery of the Holy One," for "the heart is deceitful above all things, who can know it?" Jeremiah 17:9, awe in the heart being His treasury, the Midrash affirming: "He who holds My mystery is My son". And "man is born unto toil" Job 5:7, Creation being framed in labor through a cycle of six days; yet to Israel the Sabbath was granted as a gift, conferring heart-rest, their heart being bound to Hashem across a seven-day cycle.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: And this is Deuteronomy 4:7: “For what great nation is there that has God so near unto them, as the Lord our God is in all things that we call upon Him” — showing that Israel possesses the distinction of having both Names combined, from which enduring vitality sustains the world, bounty ascending from this world to the world above from realm to realm, and subsequently descending from the highest world down to earth, as it is written (Isaiah 6:3): “And one called to another,” rendered: “and they receive one from another.”

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Ecclesiastes 10:2: ‘A sage’s mind tends toward the right hand, a fool’s toward the left.’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:52, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Ecclesiastes 10:2) to illuminate his teaching here (“and there reside the good and evil inclinations: “A wise man's heart, etc.”. However, the very inception of primal thought—is from Hashem, blessed be He, and as I wrote elsewhere on “the soul which You gave within me...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And so these two souls of Er and Onan, with whom Yehudah was occupied, to rectify the earlier corruption — only that he thought the holy bris had already been corrupted and wholly assimilated among the nations, and that there might still be hope from the side of the heart’s cleaving to Hashem. For Er and Onan are over-against the two “chambers of the heart”: “Er” corresponds to “the heart of the wise is to his right” (Koheles 10:2), where is the essence of the arousal to Hashem; and the left is from “the side of the Nukva,” where is the beginning of evil.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: And there man will not forget the Creator when receiving bounty by boasting “my power and the might of my hand”; whereas in the Diaspora, where concealment reigns, man might easily forget the Giver, so they pray regarding excessive bounty lest it confuse the mind into claiming self-made success. And upon one who recognizes that he possesses nothing of his own, the Blessed Name gazes with individual providence; for “gazing” (habatah) denotes a focused, particular intent, as in Bava Metzia (118b): “Gazing upon ownerless property acquires it,”

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: II Samuel 14:14: ‘We must all die; we are like water that is poured out on the ground and cannot be gathered up. God will not take away the life of one who makes plans so that no one may be kept banished.’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:52, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (II Samuel 14:14) to illuminate his teaching here (“as written: “and He devises means, that the banished not be cast away from Him”, and as written: “Was not Esau Jacob's brother? said Hashem, yet I loved Jacob”, without any claim or human exertion in good deeds,...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And for this reason too the Blessed Name established the phenomenon of nocturnal emission in nature, for "He devises means that the banished not be cast out from Him" (II Samuel 14:14), and through this it is rectified; and for one who sinned through wasting seed, the Blessed Name orchestrates nocturnal occurrences so that he may repent over them and this is also the secret of Yoma 86b: 'If one transgressed and repeated it, it became permitted to him—could you think so? Rather, it seems to him as permitted'; and through repenting over those later instances that appeared permitted, the earlier willful ones are automatically forgiven, and this is not the place to lengthen.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 24:7
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: Perceiving that “behold the land is large enough (rachavat yadayim)”, the acronym for Rabbi Chanina Ben Teradyon who resides there; then he knew that no banished one will be cast away, and this constitutes the essential depth of the Land of Israel (and see regarding this matter in Parashat Vayishlach at its conclusion).

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Malachi 1:2: ‘I have shown you love, said GOD. But you ask, “How have You shown us love?” After all—declares GOD—Esau is Jacob’s brother; yet I have accepted Jacob’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:52, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Malachi 1:2) to illuminate his teaching here (“and as written: “Was not Esau Jacob's brother? said Hashem, yet I loved Jacob”, without any claim or human exertion in good deeds, rather purely by way of an unearned find. And Hashem, blessed be He, testifies:”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And therefore only the pious of the nations of the world have a portion in the World to Come (Tosefta Sanhedrin 13:2), namely those who possess the reward of actual deeds performed in this world for the sake of Heaven and not for selfish benefit. Unlike Israel, regarding whom it is said: "Was not Esau Jacob's brother? says Hashem; yet I loved Jacob" (Malachi 1:2); even though they are brothers resembling one another in their external deeds, this one is beloved unconditionally without formal reason, as in "and I will be gracious to whom I will be gracious" (Shemos 33:19).
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 11:12
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: Therefore within their temporal existence there is no true life, since their entire hope is directed only to that which is fleeting. And even though they too have a contracted fear, where there shines unto them covertly a slight fear that there is a Creator ruling the world, as written (Malachi 1:11): “in every place offerings are burned and presented unto My Name... for My Name is great among the nations, etc.”

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Sanhedrin 107b: ‘Apropos the death of Elisha, the Gemara says: Until the time of Abraham there was no aging, and the old and the young looked the same. Anyone who saw Abraham said: That is Isaac, and anyone who saw Isaac said: That is Abraham. Abraham prayed for mercy, that he would undergo aging, as it is stated: “And Abraham was old, well stricken in age” (Genesis 24:1). There is no mention of aging before that verse. Until the time of Jacob there was no weakness, i.e., illness. Jacob prayed for mercy and there was weakness, as it is stated: “And one said to Joseph: Behold, your father is ill” (Genesis 48:1). Until the time of Elisha, there was no ill person who recovered, and Elisha came and prayed…’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:52, Rav Tzadok draws upon this talmudic and halakhic source (Sanhedrin 107b) to illuminate his teaching here (“and until Abraham there was no old age or exertion like his, for he “toiled and found”; yet in truth he did not need the toil, save that “the Holy One gives wisdom to the wise” specifically Daniel 2:21,”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: Nonetheless, even in this we find that Elisha was punished for it, as written in Sotah 47a and Sanhedrin 107b; and furthermore, it is not permitted to every individual, for our Sages expounded regarding Elisha (Sotah ibid.): "'And he looked upon them'—he saw that there was no good seed in them, etc."; and one who does not possess the Holy Spirit (Ruach HaKodesh) might be blinded by personal bias and resentment.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: And it is further stated there: “And on this account the world was not completed nor established in its endurance until Abraham came, etc.” — meaning that Abraham perceived and recognized that Hashem desires the endurance of the world and not its destruction. And it is further stated there: “And with all this it was not firmly planted in its roots until Jacob came and fathered twelve tribes and seventy souls” — meaning that they rectify all the shattered lights of the primordial worlds.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Daniel 2:21: ‘Who changes times and seasons,Removes kings and installs kings;Who gives the wise their wisdomAnd knowledge to those who know;’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:52, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Daniel 2:21) to illuminate his teaching here (“save that “the Holy One gives wisdom to the wise” specifically Daniel 2:21, and all His ways are just; clarifying that Abraham achieved perfection of toil, and therefore it was due to him even without toil, and this...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And the perception itself is called a "find" (metzi'ah), for in truth "Hashem gives wisdom" (Mishlei 2:6); and it is impossible for man to attain anything through his independent human strength and striving at all; but rather He "gives wisdom unto the wise" (Daniel 2:21)—and how could one be wise beforehand? Rather, this is the entire wisdom of man: his passionate longing to diligently toil to attain wisdom; and Wisdom cries out at the bustling crossroads: "I love them that love me, and those that seek me early shall find me" (Mishlei 8:17).
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: For “heavens” signify lucid clarity; hence their root is Binah (Understanding), stationed just below Chochmah, where man can consciously perceive divine glory, since human comprehension begins within the realm of Binah. “By His knowledge the depths were broken open”—notice it does not say generically “with knowledge” (be-da'at) as it says “with wisdom” and “with understanding,” but specifically “by His knowledge” (be-da'ato); which indicates that exclusively within the omniscience of the Blessed Name has the hidden deep already been cleft open.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Genesis 2:17: ‘but as for the tree of knowledge of good and bad, you must not eat of it; for as soon as you eat of it, you shall die.”’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:56, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Genesis 2:17) to illuminate his teaching here (“as written: “for in the day that you eat thereof you shall surely die”, which is the absolute ultimate of all deficiencies; for all falsehood eventually ceases to exist, as it is written: “but a lying tongue is but...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And the Holy One, blessed be He, called it 'evil' as they stated [in Sukkah 52a] from the verse 'is evil from his youth' (Bereishis 8:21), which was stated regarding the Generation of the Flood, which stems from the root of the yetzer hara in Creation via the Serpent's instigation, originating from the Blessed Name Who created the Tree of the Knowledge of Good and Evil and endowed man with free choice to eat from it, from which the feeling of physical bodily desires entered the heart, unlike their initial state wherein 'they were not ashamed' (Bereishis 2:25).
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: Therefore, throughout the creation narrative the Name Havayah is absent, employing only the Name Elohim; yet at the completion it is written (Genesis 2:4): “On the day that the Lord God (Havayah Elohim) made,” introducing the Name Havayah to teach that the ultimate fruition rests solely in the hands of the Blessed Name.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Proverbs 12:19: ‘Truthful speech abides forever,A lying tongue for but a moment.’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:56, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Proverbs 12:19) to illuminate his teaching here (“as it is written: “but a lying tongue is but for a moment”, and that is death and void; unlike the pure heart—an inheritance without borders, and when one's mouth and heart are in unison—he has no end.”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: In inverse symmetry the builders stirred to erect their Tower, but while Hashem acts with patience, evil acts with impetuous haste: "a lying tongue is but for a moment," transient like a passing cloud. Rushing prematurely into action, through which they collapsed, as when Sabbath arrived preventing the demonic bodies. Hashem declaring: "Come, let us go down...", whereupon the light of Abraham shone forth with greater radiance.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: And this is: “They that trust in the Lord are as mount Zion, which cannot be moved, but abides forever” — one who trusts only in Hashem and not in himself, making his soul like dust, possesses protection even when providence shifts attributes, never perishing. Whereas one who leans upon his own strength is consumed in that hour, fulfilling: “For the Lord your God is a jealous God,” Hashem overturning his self-reliance, leaving him devoid of life.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Numbers 23:23: ‘Lo, there is no augury in Jacob,No divining in Israel: Jacob is told at once,Yea Israel, what God has planned.’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:56, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Numbers 23:23) to illuminate his teaching here (“However, concerning Jacob it is stated: “There is no enchantment nachash in Jacob”. And this clarifies the matter of the omen nichush— that the tangible act itself contains no inherent prohibition when directed to...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: This is the level that grips the heel of Esau, concerning whom our Sages of blessed memory said (Pesikta de-Zakhor 5) that he came with the merit of the Patriarchs. That is, in the first chapter of Kiddushin (18a) he is termed an 'apostate Israelite,' for he too was circumcised at eight days. Thus he possessed the recognition and sight inherited from Abraham and Isaac, which are the preparations for Jacob's level, as explained.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: As taught in Mei HaShiloach (Vol. 1, Vayeishev, s.v. Vayeishev [2]) regarding the attribute of Jacob, who refined this balanced measure. Now behold, the Name Havayah is filled with infinite, boundless divine light, and the world cannot endure under such overwhelming radiance. Concerning this the Midrash states: “If I pour in boiling water they will burst”—for creatures cannot endure infinite light, and the shattering of the primordial worlds occurred precisely from this, as explained by the Ari in the mystery of the Shattering of the Vessels.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Bereshit Rabbah 60:7: ‘“The girl ran and told her mother’s household all about these matters” (Genesis 24:28). “The girl ran and told her mother’s household” – Rabbi Yoḥanan said: A woman frequents only her mother’s household. They raised an objection to him: “She [Rachel] told her father” (Genesis 29:12). He said to them: That was because her mother had died. To whom could she have told? Is it not to her father? “Rebecca had a brother and his name was Laban, and Laban ran out to the man, to the spring” (Genesis 24:29). “When he saw the nose ring and the bracelets upon his sister’s hands, and when he heard the words of Rebecca his sister, saying: So spoke the man to me, he came to the man and, behold, he was…’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:56, Rav Tzadok draws upon this midrashic exposition (Bereshit Rabbah 60:7) to illuminate his teaching here (“signifying that henceforth he exited the category of 'cursed' into 'blessed' Bereishit Rabbah 60:7. And this is what our Sages meant by stating that he extracted him, etc., that Laban was the one who proclaimed his...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And whoever is greater than his fellow, his casual conversation is greater than the formal Torah study of his peer, as written in Bereishit Rabbah 60:8: "More beautiful is the casual speech of the servants of the Patriarchs than the Torah of their children" and this was not Eliezer's independent virtue but Abraham's, which is why they were termed 'servants of the Patriarchs,' and in Yoma 28b: Dammasek—he draws and gives drink from the Torah of his master, for what a servant acquires his master acquires, and all Torah he possessed was termed his master's Torah.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: Therefore the Holy One, blessed be He, answered him nothing until He questioned the woman as well, and once she was held culpable, He cursed the earth on his account; and why was this? Because since the woman acted improperly, it emerged that he was aiding transgressors through his eating. Cain’s claim, however, was: “Am I my brother’s keeper?”—and surely it was not his intention to utter a lie before the Blessed Name; rather, the intent of his claim was that he was not culpable in the matter, as he could not have restrained himself from it.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Genesis 2:24: ‘Hence a man. leaves his father and mother and clings to his wife,, from ʼishshah. so that they become one flesh.’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:56, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Genesis 2:24) to illuminate his teaching here (“as written: “and they shall be one flesh”, and Isaac even from the side of physical matter was blessed; unlike Eliezer who in his physical bodily pedigree was cursed; and therefore the disparaging fact about himself...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: For concerning man and woman it is stated: "and they shall be one flesh" (Genesis 2:24), and to outward sight he is rendered like a gentile, and likewise the reverse with a woman. And self-sacrifice for this sacred separation is the root of Israel's wholeness, for: "Though He slay me, yet will I trust in Him" (Job 13:15); unlike the nations, who in the hour of distress: "fret themselves, and curse their king and their God" (Isaiah 8:21).
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: And from this, awe was etched in the survivors to uphold their word, realizing their purpose to preserve being, having witnessed the ruin of sin. And this is the depth of the Ari in Likutei Torah on: “And every shrub (siach) of the field was not yet in the earth, for the Lord God had not caused it to rain” — “Siacḥ” is an acronym for Shem, Cham, Yephet; “for He had not caused it to rain”—the Flood had not yet occurred.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Avot DeRabbi Natan 33: ‘WITH TEN TRIALS WAS ABRAHAM OUR FATHER TRIED BY THE HOLY ONE, BLESSED BE HE, AND HE WAS FOUND STEADFAST IN THEM ALL. They are: twice when he had to leave his home, 10). twice with his two sons, XXI, 10), and then in the supreme test of the binding of Isaac (ibid. XXII). twice with his two wives, XII, 15), and when he was induced to send Hagar from his home (ibid. XXI, 10). Alternatively, the second trial was the occasion when Sarah was taken by Abimelech (ibid. XX, 2). once [when he fought] against the kings, XIV. once at the Covenant between the Pieces, XV, 7ff. once in Ur of the Chaldees means ‘fire’ in Heb. and once at the Covenant of Circumcision. XVII, 10. [30a] Why [was he…’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:56, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Avot DeRabbi Natan 33) to illuminate his teaching here (“as our Sages stated Avot DeRabbi Natan 33: his two kidneys flowed with wisdom, etc., and they said of Eliezer: “he drew and gave drink to others from his master's Torah”. And deceit is also a twisted form of wisdom,”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And this is what it said: ‘until Abraham our father came and received the reward of them all’— meaning their holy sparks and their vitality, which is the holiness of the Oral Torah, and Abraham our father merited it. And this is what Rashi wrote in his commentary: " 'until Abram there was the burning wrath of the Omnipresent', for once Abraham our father came there was no longer burning wrath, since he merited and took the reward of them all, and this was written after the first trial.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: And this parallels all the ten trials wherein Abraham our Father was tested: for although the Blessed Name knows all thoughts and searches the heart, the purpose of a trial is so that the immense faith within his heart emerges into actualized reality before all; which is why it is called a “trial” (nisayon), for the tested one attains elevation (hitnasse'ut) to ascend in rank and raise a banner (nes), revealing the purity of his faith and integrity before all eyes (as explained in Parashat HaAkeidah).

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Yoma 28b: ‘When they were in Egypt there was a yeshiva with them, as it is stated: “Go and gather the Elders of Israel” (Exodus 3:16), indicating that there were Sages among them who studied Torah. And similarly, when they were in the desert, there was a yeshiva with them, as it is stated: “Gather for me seventy men from the Elders of Israel” (Numbers 11:16). Abraham our Patriarch was himself an Elder and would sit in yeshiva, as it is stated: “And Abraham was old, advanced in years” (Genesis 24:1). From the apparent redundancy of the terms old and advanced in years, it is derived that old means that he was a wise Elder and prominent in Torah, and advanced in years means that he was elderly.…’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:56, Rav Tzadok draws upon this talmudic and halakhic source (Yoma 28b) to illuminate his teaching here (“and they said of Eliezer: “he drew and gave drink to others from his master's Torah”. And deceit is also a twisted form of wisdom, only that it is titled “they are wise to do evil”, and the wisdom of Truth is the...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Ref: Ohr Zarua LaTzadik, Novellae, Rambam, Melachim 10:6 (§2)
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: If so, since Abraham had the status of a Noahide he was exempt from the 613 commandments, and performing them would incur the censure of being a hedyot, which is forbidden! – But then I found the Mordechai [Berakhot, sec. 5] on the practice of reciting the evening Shema while yet day, – writing: it is forbidden to act stringently upon oneself because of religious arrogance (yohara), and whoever is exempt and performs it is called a hedyot; thus far.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 1:29
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: But the land, whither you go over to possess it, is a land of hills and valleys, and drinks water of the rain of heaven.” And that is because in the land of Egypt they do not depend on a drop of rain, since the Nile rises and irrigates, wherefore it appears to them that through their own strength and might of hand they make themselves wealth.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Jeremiah 4:22: ‘For My people are stupid,They give Me no heed;They are foolish children,They are not intelligent.They are clever at doing wrong,But unable to do right.’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:56, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Jeremiah 4:22) to illuminate his teaching here (“only that it is titled “they are wise to do evil”, and the wisdom of Truth is the ultimate rectification of falsehood. And our Sages stated Avot 6:6: “Who is wise? He who knows his place”,”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Ref: Ohr Zarua LaTzadik, The Egyptian Exile 6:5
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: Thus in Egypt resided every discipline of knowledge and science which the Blessed Name endowed human intellect to grasp. Except that, lacking purity, it became for them an elixir of death, being "wise to do evil" [Jeremiah 4:22], calling evil good as noted from Maimonides, transforming sins into ideals: discerning the underlying metaphysical concepts of forbidden mixtures (kilayim), blood, and the like.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: And in Zohar Pekudei (267a): And here stands the harlot to entice the foolish—from which it likewise indicates that the female is the enticer. And see Likutei Torah of the Ari (Psalms 18): Know that the males are the masters of the sword and slaying, for such is nature that males are warriors; whereas the females entice man to sin; first descend the forces drawn from the female aspect of evil to seduce man, coming as females alone, for the male has not the power to seduce like the female.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Pirkei Avot 6:6: ‘Greater is learning Torah than the priesthood and than royalty, for royalty is acquired by thirty stages, and the priesthood by twenty-four, but the Torah by forty-eight things. By study, Attentive listening, Proper speech, By an understanding heart, By an intelligent heart, By awe, By fear, By humility, By joy, By attending to the sages, By critical give and take with friends, By fine argumentation with disciples, By clear thinking, By study of Scripture, By study of Mishnah, By a minimum of sleep, By a minimum of chatter, By a minimum of pleasure, By a minimum of frivolity, By a minimum of preoccupation with worldly matters, By long-suffering, By generosity, By faith in the sages, By…’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:56, Rav Tzadok draws upon this midrashic exposition (Pirkei Avot 6:6) to illuminate his teaching here (“And our Sages stated Avot 6:6: “Who is wise? He who knows his place”, which reflects the spiritual level of Truth as I wrote elsewhere; and therefore then, during that mission,”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: Therefore it states that the disciple of Rabbi Meir, who drew from his master's wellspring, stated forty-eight reasons—reflecting forty-eight distinct tastes/sensations of wisdom [just as the palate tastes food, so does the heart spiritually taste every matter of truth and righteousness, in the sense of "taste and see that Hashem is good"], corresponding to the forty-eight qualities through which the Torah is acquired (Avot 6:6); for in order for the words of Torah to become fully integrated within a person as an enduring acquisition, forty-eight attributes are required.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: And that which is taught in Avot (end of ch. 6): “Whatever the Holy One created in His world He created solely for His glory”—is formulated strictly relative to creation: that the Holy One desires to bestow upon creatures of His immense lovingkindness, that they perceive His glory and know His might. Therefore He created the cosmos in pleasant harmony so that man might perceive God's wonders, exclaiming: “How beautiful is the world, blessed is the Omnipresent who created it.”

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Genesis 24:49: ‘And now, if you mean to treat my master with true kindness, tell me; and if not, tell me also, that I may turn right or left.”’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:57, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Genesis 24:49) to illuminate his teaching here (“Genesis 24:49 “that I may turn to the right hand, or to the left”, for in every entity there exist two extremes and a middle; and Rebecca had to be a master of Chesed kindness as noted above in section 50 that this...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: Yet on the part of the remaining indelible impression—they retain a share! Wherefore the dorshei reshimot, investigating that remaining light, declared that all possess a portion in the World to Come through that enduring impression; and from this vantage it is impossible to uproot the name of Israel from a Jew; for even if uprooted through sins, the impression remains bearing the name of Israel; which can never be eradicated; unlike the nations whose root derives from the Serpent's defilement, where holiness never dwelled!
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 1:22–23
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: "And he went as Hashem had spoken unto him" (Genesis 12:4), and the Holy One called him "Avraham My friend" (Isaiah 41:8), and concerning him it was said (Psalms 110:3): "To you is the dew of your youth", for he was swift and fervent constantly in Hashem's service as in his youth, his vigor never departing. And this was derived from his being continually attached unto the Life of the Worlds, therefore he was perpetually fervent and swift; and any entity that clings to the Life of the Worlds will never grow stale nor moulder forever.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Shabbat 33b: ‘Rabbi Pineḥas ben Ya’ir, Rabbi Shimon’s son-in-law, heard and went out to greet him. He brought him into the bathhouse and began tending to his flesh. He saw that Rabbi Shimon had cracks in the skin on his body. He was crying, and the tears fell from his eyes and caused Rabbi Shimon pain. Rabbi Pineḥas said to Rabbi Shimon, his father-in-law: Woe is me, that I have seen you like this. Rabbi Shimon said to him: Happy are you that you have seen me like this, as had you not seen me like this, you would not have found in me this prominence in Torah, as the Gemara relates: At first, when Rabbi Shimon ben Yoḥai would raise a difficulty, Rabbi Pineḥas ben Ya’ir would respond to his question…’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:57, Rav Tzadok draws upon this talmudic and halakhic source (Shabbat 33b) to illuminate his teaching here (“in the manner that they stated in Shabbat 33b: “what Rabbi Elazar wounded, Rabbi Shimon healed” matching the deliberate test set by Eliezer; and kindness is generally titled 'the Right side' everywhere.”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And this explains what we find (Shabbat 33b) concerning Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai and Rabbi Elazar, when they emerged from the cave: wherever they laid their eyes was instantly consumed by fire, etc.; and afterward it is stated: as they walked on Friday afternoon, they saw an old man holding two bundles of myrtle, running at twilight; they asked him: 'What are these for?' He said: 'In honor of Shabbat, one for Zakhor and one for Shamor'; he said to his son: 'See how beloved the commandments are to Israel!' and their minds were set at ease.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: “And for man there was not found a helper opposite him. And the Lord God caused a deep sleep to fall... And the Lord God built the rib which He had taken from the man into a woman, and brought her unto the man.” And the inner meaning of this is: on behalf of all the other creatures he did not wish to lower himself in order to elevate and raise them to an exalted rung, because the gain he would derive from them after elevating them was not worth the spiritual loss that would overtake him while lowering himself to their level.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Isaiah 41:8: ‘But you, Israel, My servant,Jacob, whom I have chosen,Seed of Abraham My friend—’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:57, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Isaiah 41:8) to illuminate his teaching here (“the love of the Holy One, blessed be He—the level of “Abraham My beloved”; and love of the Torah—the level of Isaac, which is the acceptance of a disciplined yoke, as written at the end of chapter 2 of Berakhot 17a”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: In the Haftarah: "But you, Israel, are My servant, Yaakov whom I have chosen, the seed of Avraham My friend," (Isaiah 41:8), one must understand: after mentioning the name of Yaakov and Israel, why was it necessary to trace the lineage to 'the seed of Avraham'? Behold, our Sages of blessed memory stated (Bereishit Rabbah 76): "The choicest among the Patriarchs is Yaakov," and in the holy Zohar: "The praise of the Patriarchs is Yaakov" (I, 119b and other places), and likewise they taught (Bereishit Rabbah 63): "Avraham was worthy of being rescued by virtue of the merit of Yaakov,"
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 3:8 (§3)
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: And Avraham our Father refined this as his allotted portion: to illuminate every matter in conscious knowledge and reckoning, as it is written (Isaiah 41:2): "Who has raised up one from the east, called him in righteousness", and 'east' (mizrach) signifies light, and this verse is expounded concerning Avraham our Father.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Berakhot 17a: ‘Our leaders are laden. Rav and Shmuel, and some say Rabbi Yoḥanan and Rabbi Elazar, disputed the proper understanding of this verse. One said: Our leaders in Torah are laden with mitzvot. And one said: Our leaders in Torah and mitzvot are laden with suffering.’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:57, Rav Tzadok draws upon this talmudic and halakhic source (Berakhot 17a) to illuminate his teaching here (“as written at the end of chapter 2 of Berakhot 17a on the verse “our leaders laden”— which resembles submissive suffering; and in chapter Chelek Sanhedrin 101a: he makes him taste mitzvot and afflictions;”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: For the entire Torah consists of mystical Names of the Holy One, blessed be He; and this is the spiritual counsel for exile and suffering: "Exile yourself to a place of Torah" (Avot 4:14); and the Torah is called "the discipline of wisdom," for the commandments are likewise termed a "yoke" in Berakhot 17a, functioning like refining tribulations, see there.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 44:7
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: However, the essential contraction is required prior to union, and following union is the primary demand for awe, as written (Malachi 2:5): “and was afraid before My name”— meaning prior to My Name, whereas within My Name itself it is full of goodness. As brought in the holy Zohar (Eikev 271b): one bows his head at 'Attah' (You), but at Havayah straightens his head, as likewise taught in the Talmud (Berakhot 12a).

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Psalms 144:14: ‘our cattle are well cared for.There is no breaching and no sortie,and no wailing in our streets.’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:57, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Psalms 144:14) to illuminate his teaching here (“on the verse “our leaders laden”— which resembles submissive suffering; and in chapter Chelek Sanhedrin 101a: he makes him taste mitzvot and afflictions; and so it is titled 'the yoke of Torah'”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: That is, there in the “heel” is hidden the “beginning of thought” and the root of David — corresponding to the World of Asiyah [Action], which is the perfection of the deed. — so that the very lowest “heel,” where Esav took hold, is precisely where the root of David lay hidden, and whence Mashiach will yet rise.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: From this very awareness, however, all forms of awe sprout forth: because he recognizes the boundless greatness of the Blessed Name, he desires intensely to refine and clarify himself; for from his own side as well, man longs to remain cleaving to the Blessed Name throughout all his active deeds; and therefore, with each particular action a person trembles lest he is not truly cleaving within that specific detail to the illumination of Hashem; and even if he perceives that in this single detail he is wholly cleaving, he fears lest he fails to cleave to Hashem's light in another detail.

Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: Yet after they were shattered, their cry ascended on high, as Scripture states (Psalms 102:11): “For You have lifted me up, and cast me down.” Therefore afterward emerged the World of Rectification, for that heartfelt cry is considered “the toil of your hands.” So too here: “Ten Utterances for the Giving of the Torah”—the legions of the Tabernacle represent the toil of hands, for in the Tabernacle they exerted themselves.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Shabbat 119b: ‘Rav Ḥisda said that Mar Ukva said: One who prays on Shabbat evening and recites vaykhullu, the two ministering angels who accompany the person at all times place their hands on his head and say to him: “And your iniquity has passed, and your sin has been atoned” (Isaiah 6:7). It was taught in a baraita: Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda says: Two ministering angels accompany a person on Shabbat evening from the synagogue to his home, one good angel and one evil angel. And when he reaches his home and finds a lamp burning and a table set and his bed made, the good angel says: May it be Your will that it shall be like this for another Shabbat. And the evil angel answers against his will: Amen. And if…’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:65, Rav Tzadok draws upon this talmudic and halakhic source (Shabbat 119b) to illuminate his teaching here (“as our Sages noted in Shabbat 119b; and Shabbat is the rung of King David, where admission and submission become unavoidable, as written of King Solomon who reigned even over demons who were subjugated to him Gittin 68b.”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: Now every Friday night we sing 'Peace be unto you, ministering angels.' At first glance this is founded on Shabbos 119b, which says that two angels accompany a person from synagogue to home on the eve of Shabbos; but that passage describes one angel as good and the other otherwise. We may explain it in light of Chagigah 14b, when the Sages expounded the Work of the Chariot.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 4:4 (§2)
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: And that is: before an intensified holiness became strictly essential to him, there had not been channeled unto him a surplus of holy blessing that would remain superfluous, for why should he have it?! However, upon his descent into Egypt, dread surrounding him from entering it, and he was thirsting for the salvation of Hashem, Hashem awakened the holiness in the depth of his heart, expanding and surging in might, and then he saw and perceived that he could endure through it even there.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Gittin 68b: ‘With regard to the verse: “And this was my portion from all of my toil” (Ecclesiastes 2:10), the Gemara asks: What is the meaning of the expression: “And this”? This expression is always an allusion to an item that is actually in his hand or can be shown. Rav and Shmuel disagree with regard to the meaning of this phrase. One said: This is referring to Solomon’s staff that remained in his hand. And one said: This is referring to his cloak. Solomon circulated from door to door collecting charity, and wherever he arrived he would say: “I, Ecclesiastes, was king over Israel in Jerusalem” (Ecclesiastes 1:12). When he finally arrived at the Sanhedrin in Jerusalem the sages said: Now, an…’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:65, Rav Tzadok draws upon this talmudic and halakhic source (Gittin 68b) to illuminate his teaching here (“as written of King Solomon who reigned even over demons who were subjugated to him Gittin 68b. And this is what is written: “and said unto him: We have found water”, and Scripture does not say “and they found water”,...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: Wherefore when our father Jacob perceived his immense holiness ("an adder in the path", Bereishis 49:17), he imagined that he would never die and was King Mashiach! However, those who are submerged in the lusts of this world of falsehood are likewise designated "lame"; for "falsehood has no feet," as stated in Shabbat (104a); and as known in the mystery of: "her feet go down to death" (Mishlei 5:5), where resides the primary dominion of the husks; the feet symbolizing the organs of lust: "he had neither dressed his feet" (II Shmuel 19:25), and "at her feet he bowed, he fell, he lay" (Shoftim 5:27).
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: And this explains King Solomon's proverb: “Though you bray a fool in a mortar...”: with every clever scheme the succeeding generations devised after seeing the downfall of their predecessors, their foolishness departed not; all seeking only lawless expansion, each generation inventing a new stratagem to escape Hashem's hand: the Generation of Enosh embraced dark concealment to flee from their Master; the Generation of the Flood embraced unchecked expansion, trading eternity for fleeting lust, wherefore “the earth was filled with violence”.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Genesis 26:32: ‘That same day Isaac’s servants came and told him about the well they had dug, and said to him, “We have found water!”’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:65, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Genesis 26:32) to illuminate his teaching here (“And this is what is written: “and said unto him: We have found water”, and Scripture does not say “and they found water”, because the finding had not yet materialized in ultimate tangible reality and concerning the...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: Arriving at absolute cleaving unto the Blessed Name, which is the perception of ultimate truth devoid of any illusion whatsoever, this being the mystery of the letter Hei. And the letter Kuf is that which mimics it like an ape before a human, meaning that which lies within human capacity through personal exertion in this world; for the letter Kuf signifies "holy" (kadosh), as written in Shabbos (104a); and in holiness this represents man striving to resemble the Most High, as it is written: "Sanctify yourselves therefore, and be you holy; for I am holy" (Vayikra 11:44).
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: And they said that it would be better for them to be left in the hands of His blessed will, without any power of free choice at all, through the laws of nature engraved in each and every one, about which they were confident that no flaw or deficiency would be found in them, for they have a claim, as stated (Ta’anit 20b): “Go to the Craftsman who made me.”

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Bereshit Rabbah 64:11: ‘“The Lord will not starve the soul of the righteous” (Proverbs 10:3) – this is Isaac. “Reside in this land.” “And He averts the devastation of the wicked” (Proverbs 10:3) – this is Avimelekh. “There was a famine” – Ten famines came to the world. One during the days of Adam the first man – “accursed is the ground because of you” (Genesis 3:17); one during the days of Lemekh – “from the ground that the Lord had cursed” (Genesis 5:29); one during the days of Abraham – “there was famine in the land and Abram descended to Egypt” (Genesis 12:10); one during the days of Isaac: “there was a famine in the land”; one during the days of Jacob – “for these two years there has been famine” (Genesis…’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:65, Rav Tzadok draws upon this midrashic exposition (Bereshit Rabbah 64:11) to illuminate his teaching here (“And this is what our Sages said Bereishit Rabbah, end of section 64:11: “We do not know whether they found water or did not find water, etc.”, meaning: along the lines of what I heard on the teaching of our Sages at...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: However, regarding the divine souls themselves, our Sages expounded on the verse, "These were the potters that dwelt with the King for His work," that with them the Holy One took counsel, for they preceded the creation of the world, because they are an emanation from the very essence of Hashem, may He be blessed. It is only the animalistic soul—which serves as the outer garment—that was created on the second day from the side of Gevurah, when the angels were brought into existence as taught in Bereishit Rabbah.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: “These are the generations of Noah, etc.” It is written (Job 26:11): “The pillars of heaven tremble and are astonished at His rebuke.” This verse refers to the devastation of the Flood, for through the rebuke Hashem struck against the Generation of the Flood, creation was fortified. For rebuke is one of the ten instruments through which the Holy One created the world (Chagigah 12a); and this cosmic rebuke occurred during the Flood, after which the foundations of creation were strengthened, having previously been fragile and unsteady.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Bava Metzia 3a: ‘The Gemara comments: And the tanna of the mishna also taught a similar halakha: In a case of two people who came to court holding a garment, where this one says: I found it, and the other one says: I found it, each litigant takes an oath and they divide the garment. And here, in the case of a found item, since each litigant is holding part of the garment, it is clear to us that what is in this one’s grasp is his, and what is in that one’s grasp is his. This is tantamount to witnesses testifying that part of the claim of each litigant is legitimate. And the mishna teaches that each of them takes an oath.’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:65, Rav Tzadok draws upon this talmudic and halakhic source (Bava Metzia 3a) to illuminate his teaching here (“meaning: along the lines of what I heard on the teaching of our Sages at the beginning of Bava Metzia 3a: I would have thought: what does “I found it” mean? I saw it, etc., for in popular idiom mere seeing is termed...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And the returning echo of prayer is illustrated in Ta'anit and Bava Metzia: he said, "He causes the wind to blow"—and the wind blew; "He causes the rain to fall"—and rain descended; this being the returning echo of his prayer. And the Bat Kol issuing from the mouth of Hashem operates likewise, the speech of Hashem being tantamount to action (Shabbat 119b), and instantly the wind blew and rain fell by virtue of Hashem's Bat Kol; and likewise Berakhot (7a): "From where do we derive that the Holy One prays?"—meaning that through Israel's prayers they generate a returning echo Above.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: A perception standing closer to the light where one takes active possession is the aspect of Reshut, requiring careful spiritual screening; and this is Black Fire, which possesses defined shape and color, analogous to tasting which demands rigorous purification. This was the level of those who entered the Land of Israel: just as each had landed inheritance, so each held individual grasp in Torah, and Hashem was revealed to them as Black Fire, representing the internalization of divine bounty into tangible life.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Genesis 26:32: ‘That same day Isaac’s servants came and told him about the well they had dug, and said to him, “We have found water!”’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:65, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Genesis 26:32) to illuminate his teaching here (“Save that Scripture records: “and they found a well of springing water”, as I wrote above multiple times that Abraham and David are one: Abraham is the inception of Thought, and David the culmination of Action;”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And he was rescued solely in the merit that from him would issue the Jewish nation, receivers of the Torah, and Moses our teacher, and the like. And since it was necessary that one survive for the preservation of the world so that they emerge from him, he remained, who was righteous in his generations. However the Torah came to teach us that in truth the righteous are not called after his name, for they are called the children of Abraham who was like a newborn child; and one who vows against the descendants of Noah is permitted to Jews.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: And because the feet are capable of carrying a person exceedingly far, until he steps outside the boundary (techum) and forgets the origin whence he came, therefore Scripture warns: “If you restrain your foot because of the Sabbath” — meaning that upon reaching the boundary he should remind himself of the holy light of the Sabbath, pulling back his feet from extending any further outward, and returning to the inception, to the source whence he departed.
